## Purpose

This SOP establishes the physical documentation standards for
laboratory notebooks in the EA Program. A properly maintained notebook
is a legal record that establishes what was done, when, by whom, and
what was observed. These standards follow Good Documentation Practice
(GDP) principles used in regulated laboratories and ensure that EA
Program data are traceable, contemporaneous, and defensible
[@kanare1985; @usepa2002qapp].

This SOP covers *how* to record. For *what* to record during an
analytical session, see
[SOP-L802 Quality Control](SOP-L802-quality-control.qmd), Section 7.1.
For field notebook protocols, see
[SOP-F003 Field Notebook Protocols](../field_sops/SOP-F003-field-notebook-protocols.qmd).


## Scope

- **Applies to:** All laboratory work performed under EA Program SOPs,
  including sample preparation, instrument operation, calibration,
  data reduction, and reagent/standard preparation
- **Does not apply to:** Field notebooks (see
  [SOP-F003](../field_sops/SOP-F003-field-notebook-protocols.qmd)) or
  purely electronic records in R scripts and Git (see
  [SOP-L801](SOP-L801-rstudio-github.qmd)), though electronic records
  should meet the same traceability standards [@fda_part11_2004]
- **Location:** All EA Program laboratories (SGM 133, 134, 135)


## Responsibilities

| Role               | Responsibility                                         |
|:-------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|
| Lab PI             | Set documentation standards; review notebooks          |
| Lab Manager        | Issue notebooks; maintain archive; verify compliance   |
| All Lab Personnel  | Maintain a notebook per this SOP                       |
| New Students       | Read this SOP before beginning any lab work            |


## Definitions

- **Archival ink:** Ink formulated to resist fading, water, and
  chemical degradation over decades; required for all permanent
  laboratory notebook entries; ballpoint or pigment-based pens are
  preferred over roller-ball gel inks [@kanare1985].
- **Carbon-copy notebook:** A notebook with interleaved carbonless
  copy pages that produce a duplicate of each entry; the copy is torn
  out and stored separately as a backup, while the original remains
  bound in the notebook.
- **Contemporaneous record:** An entry made at the time the
  observation or action occurs, not reconstructed from memory
  afterward; the defining characteristic of a legally defensible
  laboratory record [@kanare1985].
- **GDP (Good Documentation Practice):** A set of principles for
  creating accurate, legible, contemporaneous, original, and
  attributable records; the foundation of data integrity in regulated
  and research laboratories [@usepa2002qapp].
- **Single-strikethrough correction:** The required method for
  correcting an error in a laboratory notebook: draw a single line
  through the incorrect entry so it remains legible, write the correct
  entry nearby, and sign and date the correction; erasing or using
  white-out is prohibited [@kanare1985].
- **Table of Contents (TOC):** A running index of entries, maintained
  on the first 2 pages of every notebook, linking dates and topics to
  page numbers; enables rapid retrieval of specific entries.
- **Witness signature:** A second person's signature and date on a
  notebook entry confirming that they observed or reviewed the work;
  required for patent-related records and recommended for any
  significant observation.


## Required Notebook Type

Use a bound, carbon-copy laboratory notebook with numbered pages (e.g.,
a 200-page carbonless copy notebook). Do not use spiral-bound
notebooks, loose-leaf paper, or stapled pages as primary records. The
carbon-copy notebook provides a built-in backup: the copy page is
removed and stored separately, and the original remains permanently
bound [@kanare1985].

Acceptable notebooks are available from the lab manager. Notify the
lab manager when you are on the last 20 pages so a replacement can be
ordered.


## Setting Up a New Notebook

1. Write your name, contact information, the notebook serial number
   (if present), and the start date on the outside spine.
2. On the inside front cover, record: your name, contact information,
   project name, and the date the notebook was put into service.
3. Reserve the first two pages for a Table of Contents. Update the TOC
   as you fill the notebook.


## Writing Instruments

### Required

Write **all** entries in permanent, non-erasable ink [@kanare1985].
Use a ballpoint pen that produces a clear impression on both the
original and the carbon-copy page. Black or dark blue ink is
preferred.

### Not Permitted

- Pencil (can be erased)
- Gel ink or felt-tip pens that do not transfer reliably to the carbon
  copy
- Erasable ink pens

::: {.callout-tip}
Test your pen on a spare carbon-copy page before starting a new
notebook. Press firmly enough to produce a legible duplicate, but not
so hard that you tear the paper.
:::


## Entry Formatting

### Every Entry Begins With

At the top of each new entry (or new day), record:

1. **Date** in ISO format: YYYY-MM-DD (e.g., 2026-05-18)
2. **Your name** (or initials, if your full name is on the inside cover
   and you are the sole user)
3. **Purpose** of the work session in one sentence (e.g., "TOC-L
   calibration and K~2~SO~4~ extract analysis, Project: BFS Soils")
4. **SOP(s) in use** with revision numbers

### Contemporaneous Recording

Write entries **at the time the work is performed**, not from memory
afterward [@kanare1985]. If you record a result on a printout, sticky
note, or scrap paper during an urgent moment, tape or staple the
original into the notebook and initial and date it at the earliest
opportunity. Never discard the original note.

### Level of Detail

Write enough detail so that another trained researcher could reproduce
your work using only the notebook and the referenced SOP. At minimum,
include all items listed in
[SOP-L802, Section 7.1](SOP-L802-quality-control.qmd)
[@usepa2002qapp].

### Printouts, Graphs, and Attachments

Tape or staple instrument printouts, chromatograms, calibration
reports, or other documents directly into the notebook. Write across
the border of the attachment and the notebook page so that it is clear
the attachment was placed at that time. Initial and date each
attachment.

### Tables and Calculations

- Draw tables with a ruler if practical.
- Show all calculations, including units and intermediate steps, so
  that results can be verified.
- Circle or box final results for easy identification.

### Blank Space and Unused Pages

- Do not leave large blank areas within an entry. If you finish an
  entry partway down a page, draw a diagonal line through the remaining
  blank space and initial and date it. This prevents later additions.
- Never skip pages. If you accidentally skip a page, draw a diagonal
  line through it, write "INTENTIONALLY LEFT BLANK," and initial and
  date it [@kanare1985].


## Error Correction

If you make a mistake in the notebook [@kanare1985]:

1. Draw a **single horizontal line** through the incorrect text so it
   remains legible.
2. Write the correct information directly above, below, or beside the
   crossed-out entry.
3. Write your initials and the date next to the correction.
4. If the error is extensive (e.g., an entire wrong entry), strike
   through the full section, write "Error -- see page XX," and rewrite
   the correct entry on the next available page.

::: {.callout-important}
### Prohibited Correction Methods
- White-out, correction tape, or liquid paper
- Erasing or scratching out (even when using pencil)
- Tearing out or cutting out pages
- Writing over an existing entry

Any of these actions raises data integrity concerns and may invalidate
the record [@kanare1985].
:::


## Electronic Data References

When analysis is performed electronically (R scripts, instrument
software, spreadsheets), record in the notebook:

- The name and location of the electronic file (e.g., full file path
  or GitHub repository URL)
- The date and time the file was created or the analysis was run
- The software version or R version used

Cross-referencing electronic records ensures that the notebook and the
digital record are linked and neither stands alone
[@fda_part11_2004; @usepa2002qapp].


## Carbon-Copy Management

1. After completing each session, remove the carbon-copy page.
2. Review the copy for legibility. If the copy is not readable, note
   this on the original and on the copy.
3. Place the copy in the project's designated folder on the lab shared
   drive or in the physical project file.
4. The original stays bound in the notebook permanently.


## Signature and Witness

- Sign and date each entry when you complete it.
- If your work produces a significant new observation or result (a new
  datum, a method validation, a reproducibility test), have a witness
  (a labmate or the PI) sign and date the entry as well.
- For IP-sensitive work, all entries should be witnessed at the time of
  writing, not retroactively.


## Carbon Copy Storage and Notebook Archiving

### Carbon Copies

File carbon copies chronologically in the project file within 48 hours
of each session. Label the folder clearly with the project name, PI,
and date range.

### Full Notebooks

When a notebook is full:

1. Record the completion date on the outside spine.
2. Update the Table of Contents on the first two pages.
3. File the completed notebook in the **Notebook Archive** (SGM 133,
   labeled shelf), organized by project and date.
4. Update the Notebook Registry spreadsheet with the completion date.
5. Notebooks are retained for a minimum of **7 years** after the end
   of the associated project, or longer if required by a funding
   agency, IRB, or regulatory body.
6. Notebooks are the property of the EA Program and Pomona College.
   They must not be taken home, discarded, or removed from the archive
   without PI approval [@kanare1985].


## Common Mistakes

| Mistake                                  | Consequence                              |
|:-----------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Using pencil                             | Entries can be erased; not a permanent record |
| Recording data on scratch paper first    | Scratch paper gets lost; transcription adds errors |
| Leaving entries unsigned                 | Cannot confirm who performed the work    |
| Leaving blank space without striking through | Appearance that data could be inserted later |
| Using white-out or scribbling over errors | Raises data integrity concerns          |
| Not removing carbon-copy duplicates      | Backup is only useful if stored separately |
| Forgetting to reference electronic files | Data become disconnected from context    |
| Skipping the Table of Contents           | Information is hard to locate later      |

## Training Record

Before beginning independent laboratory work, all personnel must:

1. Read this SOP in full
2. Set up a new notebook correctly (inside cover, Table of Contents,
   registry entry)
3. Demonstrate a properly formatted entry including: header, data
   recording, attached printout, error correction, blank-space
   management, and signature
4. Be signed off by the lab manager or PI
